summary: Defines new CBOR tags for representing calendar dates, building on the time tags in the original CBOR specification. One tag carries a date as a count of days relative to an epoch, and another carries it as a text string, so applications can send a date without a time of day.

eli5.summary: CBOR is a compact way to write down data. This adds clear labels so a computer can tell that a value is a plain calendar date, like a birthday, rather than a moment in time.

how to encode a calendar date in cbor
subtitle: Two CBOR tags for sending a calendar date with no time of day, as text or as a day count.

tldr.problem: CBOR already had tags for moments in time, but some applications, such as a date of birth on a driver's license, need a date with no time of day or time zone.
tldr.mechanism: Tag 1004 wraps a text string in the RFC 3339 full-date form, and tag 100 wraps an integer counting days since 1970-01-01 in the Gregorian calendar.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now mark a value as a plain calendar date. Because a date is not a point in time, using it for decisions such as access control needs care.

today: RFC 8943 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the reference document for the IANA registration of CBOR tags 1004 and 100.

sections.title: Dates Without Times in CBOR
sections.content:
The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), defined in RFC 7049, lets programs exchange structured data without a pre-agreed schema. It also has a tagging mechanism, with tags registered in an IANA registry, that extends the set of data types.

RFC 7049 defines tag 0 (a date/time string as per RFC 3339) and tag 1 (POSIX seconds since the epoch). RFC 8943 adds two tags for a date without a time. Because there is no time, times of day, time zones and leap seconds do not apply. Both tags are for dates in the Gregorian calendar.
sections.eli5: CBOR already had labels for 'this exact moment.' This adds labels for 'this day,' like a birthday on the calendar.

sections.title: The Two Date Tags
sections.content:
The first tag, 1004, wraps a UTF-8 text string written as the RFC 3339 full-date production, for example "1940-10-09".

The second tag, 100 (the ASCII letter 'd'), wraps an unsigned or negative integer: the number of days since the Gregorian calendar date 1970-01-01. As an implementation note, this value is the Modified Julian Date minus 40587.

The epoch of tag 100 is related to the POSIX time epoch 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z only because both contain the date 1970-01-01. A value using this tag does not stand for any time of day or time zone.
sections.eli5: One label writes the day out as words and digits. The other just counts how many days have passed since a starting day, and counts backwards for older dates.

sections.title: Example Dates
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples, using the birth and death dates of John Lennon.

DateTag 1004Tag 100
October 9, 1940"1940-10-09"-10676
December 8, 1980"1980-12-08"3994

The earlier date comes before 1970-01-01, so its day count is negative.
sections.eli5: A date before the starting day gets a minus sign, like counting backwards on a calendar.

sections.title: Comparing Dates
sections.content:
Dates in full-date format can be compared with normal string comparison, because the digits are in a fixed format and run from most significant to least significant. Numeric dates counting days since 1970-01-01 can be compared with normal integer comparison.

Comparing dates in other formats or calendars needs conversions that are beyond the scope of the RFC, and so is comparing a date with a date/time value. The RFC notes that the day of the week is not represented in either format, though algorithms outside its scope can derive it.

A date can match different moments depending on the time zone. At many times of the day, Japan's Friday corresponds with Hawaii's Thursday.
sections.eli5: Dates written the same way sort neatly, like numbers on a list. But 'today' is not the same moment everywhere on Earth.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7049 apply, and the new tags are not expected to raise more. The RFC adds that a date itself has significant security considerations, including exploitation of ambiguities where the date matters to security or access control.

Since a calendar date is not a specific point in time, a decision based on it can differ by place. A person may have reached their 21st birthday in Japan while being a day short of it in Hawaii. For the same reason, it would be inappropriate to use only a date to trigger certificate expiration.
sections.eli5: If a rule says 'you are old enough today,' the answer can differ depending on where in the world you ask.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers both tags in the IANA 'Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Tags' registry and is the reference document for them.

  • Tag 1004: data item is a UTF-8 text string; semantics are an RFC 3339 full-date string.
  • Tag 100: data item is an unsigned or negative integer; semantics are the number of days since the epoch date 1970-01-01.
sections.eli5: The two labels were written in an official list so everyone uses the same numbers for the same meaning.

references.text: Klyne, G. and C. Newman, "Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps", RFC 3339, July 2002.
